A1.justification: Both PDFs describe TARS by the same authors. Their complete main texts, appendices, equations, tables, and figures are readable and support reliable matching despite extensive reformatting and expansion.

before.justification: v1 reports original LLaVA-7B/13B evaluations, component and hyperparameter ablations, representation analyses, and qualitative comparisons.

after.justification: v4 retains those empirical results and adds augmentation, retrieval, training-dynamics, broader benchmark, and Muffin-13B experiments.

M1.justification: The stated spectral objective changes substantively in Eq. (11): v1 repeats the preferred-response policy term in both log numerators, cancelling policy dependence; v4 uses the rejected response in the second numerator. This repairs a central training loss, although the PDFs do not establish whether implementation changed or experiments were rerun. The underlying token-selection and perturbation mechanisms remain.

E1.justification: Beyond the retained four hallucination benchmarks, v4 adds MS-COCO captioning evaluation, LLaVA-Bench conversation/detail/reasoning tasks, and SeedBench multiple-choice visual reasoning (Section 10.2). It also evaluates explicitly perturbed held-out inputs in the new robustness study.

E2.justification: The Table 1 comparator set is retained. New comparisons evaluate back-translation and LLM augmentation baselines, RE-ALIGN, spatial l2/cosine regularizers, and random/high-visual-relevance perturbation controls. The token-level contrastive comparator already appeared in v1 and is retained in v4 Table 15.

E3.justification: v4 introduces a separate 20-epoch training-dynamics protocol with normalized losses and clean/perturbed held-out evaluation, augmentation experiments using 9.6k and 28.8k training samples, Muffin-13B configurations, and three MS-COCO captioning protocols. The original three-epoch LLaVA training setup and greedy decoding remain documented unchanged.

E4.justification: New analyses test whether adaptive token targeting beats random or visually relevant targeting, whether FFT alignment beats l2/cosine alternatives, and whether min-max training improves clean and perturbed generalization (Sections 9.4–9.6). Augmentation and retrieval combination studies additionally test complementarity. Earlier component, data-scale, hyperparameter, contrastive-alignment, and qualitative analyses are retained.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, error bars, or significance tests for the experimental results. The added 20-epoch curves describe training duration and dynamics, not repeated-run uncertainty.

E6.justification: Table 1 scores remain unchanged, but v4 adds substantial results under new settings, including TARS scores of 67.2 on LLaVA-Bench and 38.7% on SeedBench, and 16.2% AMBER hallucination rate for Muffin-13B with masking. New augmentation, retrieval, and control results further expand the findings. The main-text 13B hallucination-rate statement is corrected from 12.7% to the retained table value of 12.5%.

T1.justification: Section 9.3 adds bounded single-token perturbation assumptions, a spectral-energy proposition and proof, a Parseval derivation, and a low-frequency masking theorem absent from v1. This is substantive formal development. The theorem analyzes a masked squared spectral distance, distinct from the main log-ratio loss in Eq. (11).

C1.justification: v4 makes superiority to data scaling a central claim, asserting that adversarial optimization is fundamentally more effective than augmentation based on the 28.8k-sample comparison. It also claims theoretically principled spectral invariance and preservation of broader reasoning capabilities. These extend v1's central claims about efficient hallucination reduction and visual grounding.

C2.justification: v4 adds explanations linking low-frequency components to global semantics, training dynamics to implicit regularization, and augmentation/retrieval complementarity to different sources of hallucination. These materially extend the mechanism discussion. Existing limitations concerning simple perturbations and heuristic token relevance remain substantially unchanged.

D1.justification: v4 adds concrete specifications for GPT-3.5-Turbo back-translation through Chinese/French, Vicuna-13B generation with CLIP filtering, and top-three CLIP-based retrieval. Existing hardware, core hyperparameters, and training-time disclosures remain. v1's project-page link is omitted, without establishing any change in actual resource availability.

R1.justification: Most of the MLLM and DPO literature discussion is retained. v4 adds adversarial-training positioning, discusses its relationship to RE-ALIGN, and adds references supporting the new benchmarks and Muffin experiments; the PaLM-E reference is removed. This is a limited expansion of the existing research positioning.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, contribution list, and conclusion are substantially rewritten around spectral justification and optimization versus augmentation. Appendix discussions are condensed and reorganized, the algorithm presentation is shortened, and references move from before the appendix to the document end.

P2.justification: The document changes from a two-column layout to a narrower single-column format with extensively resized tables and figures. v4 adds training-dynamics plots and several experimental tables, moves the MMHal breakdown into the main text, and relabels the retained qualitative comparison from Table 8 to Figure 8. Augmentation results are displayed in both Tables 3 and 12.

improvement.justification: Correcting the cancelling spectral loss and adding targeted controls and broader capability tests improve specification and empirical scrutiny. However, new augmentation Tables 3 and 12 conflict—for example, TARS plus 5x augmentation has OBJHal CRi of 2.7 versus 2.9—and the new theorem concerns a different loss from Eq. (11). The sweeping superiority-to-data-scaling claim also exceeds the tested augmentation regimes. These issues limit the net quality gain.
